title: EU Blue Card: Who qualifies and how to apply | Grey
summary: See who qualifies for the EU Blue Card and how to apply. Degree and salary thresholds, plus the German route, explained. Start your application today.
body_markdown:
Moving to Europe for work can feel complicated when you are trying to understand which visa, residence permit and eligibility requirements apply to you. The EU Blue Card offers a route for highly qualified non-EU nationals who have the skills and qualifications European employers need.


To qualify for an EU Blue Card, you generally need a recognised university degree or equivalent professional qualification, a qualifying employment contract or job offer, and a salary that meets the required threshold in the EU country where you plan to work. Requirements can vary between countries, so checking the rules for your destination matters before you apply.


The EU Blue Card combines the right to live and work in a participating EU country with a pathway to greater mobility within the EU. Understanding the eligibility criteria, salary requirements and application process can help you decide whether it is the right route for your move.

### **What is the EU Blue Card?**


The EU Blue Card is a work and residence permit for highly qualified non-EU nationals who have a qualifying job offer in a participating European Union country. It is designed to attract skilled professionals from outside the EU by giving them the right to live and work in the country where they are employed, provided they meet the required qualifications, salary and employment conditions.


The “highly qualified” requirement generally means you need higher education qualifications, such as a recognised university degree, or qualifying professional skills recognised under the rules of the country where you apply. You also need a binding job offer or employment contract that meets the required salary threshold. Because these thresholds and application requirements vary by country, your eligibility can depend on where you plan to work.


Most EU countries participate in the EU Blue Card scheme, including Germany, France, the Netherlands, Spain and Italy. Denmark and Ireland do not participate, so you need to consider the specific immigration route available in your chosen destination before applying.


## **Who qualifies for the EU Blue Card?**


You may qualify for the EU Blue Card if you are a highly qualified non-EU national with a qualifying job offer in a participating EU country. You generally need higher professional qualifications, a work contract or binding job offer lasting at least six months, and a salary that meets your destination country’s threshold.


A university degree is the most common way to meet the qualification requirement, typically through a recognised higher education programme of at least three years. However, some countries also recognise relevant professional experience as an alternative, particularly for certain occupations such as IT. Your job must also match the qualifications or professional skills you are using to qualify for the card.


There is no single euro salary figure for the whole EU. Under the current rules, each participating country sets its own threshold, generally between 1 and 1.6 times its average gross annual salary. For example, Germany’s 2026 threshold is €50,700, with a lower €45,934.20 threshold for shortage occupations and certain recent graduates.


## **The Blue Card in Germany**


Germany is the largest issuer of EU Blue Cards in Europe, making it an important destination for highly qualified professionals looking to work in the EU. In 2024, Germany issued 56,252 Blue Cards, representing 72% of all cards issued across the EU.


For 2026, the standard salary threshold in Germany is €50,700 gross per year. A lower threshold of €45,934.20 applies to shortage occupations, provided the Federal Employment Agency approves the employment. Recent graduates can also qualify at the lower threshold, while certain IT specialists may qualify without a university degree if they have the required professional experience.


Germany’s shortage occupations include academic STEM professionals, doctors, veterinarians, dentists, pharmacists, nurses and midwives, teachers and educators, as well as certain managers in manufacturing, logistics, ICT and professional services. This means that when searching for[German companies that sponsor work visas](https://grey.co/blog/germany-companies-sponsor-work-visa) , your occupation and the salary offered can directly affect your EU Blue Card eligibility.


## **How to apply for the EU Blue Card step by step**


Once you have confirmed that you qualify, the EU Blue Card application usually follows a straightforward sequence, although the exact process depends on the country where you will work.


1. Secure a qualifying job: Get a signed employment contract or binding job offer that meets the required salary threshold and runs for at least six months.
2. Prepare your documents: Gather your valid passport, employment contract, CV, degree certificates, proof of qualifications and health insurance. Your destination country may require foreign documents to be translated, legalised or accompanied by a statement of comparability.
3. Apply for the required visa: If you need an entry visa, submit your application through the relevant embassy or consulate in your country of residence, including your supporting documents and biometrics.
4. Enter your destination country: Once your visa is approved, travel to the country where you will work and complete any required address registration or other local formalities.
5. Apply for your Blue Card: Depending on the country and your circumstances, you may apply before travelling or after arrival. The immigration authority reviews your application and, once approved, issues your biometric EU Blue Card residence permit.

## **EU Blue Card benefits and path to permanent residence**


The EU Blue Card offers more than permission to work, giving you options for family reunification, mobility across participating EU countries and eventually permanent residence.


### **Family reunification**


Your EU Blue Card can make it easier to bring eligible family members to join you in your destination country. Spouses and dependent children may qualify for residence permits, with specific rights depending on national rules. In many cases, family members can also access employment without needing a separate work permit, helping your household settle more easily.


### **EU mobility**


After legally living in an EU country with an EU Blue Card, you can gain greater mobility within participating EU countries. After 12 months of legal residence in your first member state, you may be able to move to another participating country for highly qualified employment, although you must apply for a new Blue Card under that country’s rules.


### **Path to permanent residence**


The EU Blue Card can also contribute towards long-term residence, although the timeline depends on your circumstances and national rules. Under EU rules, Blue Card holders can generally qualify for EU long-term resident status after five years of continuous legal residence, with periods spent in other participating EU countries potentially counting towards the requirement.

## **Frequently asked questions**


### **What is the EU Blue Card?**


The EU Blue Card is a work and residence permit for highly qualified non-EU citizens who want to live and work in participating EU countries. It provides a legal route to employment for professionals who meet the required education, salary and job conditions in their chosen destination.


### **Who is eligible?**


You may qualify as a non-EU professional with a recognised higher education qualification and a qualifying employment contract or binding job offer. In certain cases, particularly for IT professionals, relevant professional experience can replace a traditional degree, depending on the country’s rules.


### **What salary do I need?**


Your salary must meet the threshold set by the country where you will work. Under EU rules, the threshold generally falls between 1.0 and 1.6 times the national average gross annual salary, with lower thresholds potentially applying to shortage occupations and other qualifying groups.


### **Which countries offer it?**


The EU Blue Card is available in 25 EU member states. Denmark and Ireland do not participate in the EU Blue Card scheme, so professionals planning to work there need to explore their separate national work and residence routes instead.


### **Can my family join me?**


Yes. Your eligible family members can generally join you through family reunification procedures, and EU Blue Card rules provide favourable conditions for accompanying family members. Spouses may also have access to employment, although the exact application process and requirements depend on the country where you live.


### **How do I send money?**
